strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a useful evaluation gap: Chinese multi-day, multi-POI planning with detailed temporal, transportation, dining, and accommodation constraints. The sandbox covers 10 cities and thousands of POIs.
The inclusion of 154 human-derived queries alongside 450 synthetic queries is valuable for studying requirements beyond fixed generation templates.
Executable, compositional constraints and quantitative preference objectives offer greater flexibility than a fixed checklist of requirements.

The experiments include three LLMs, oracle-translation comparisons, and preference ablations. The reported human-query results—27.9% final pass rate versus 2.6% for the strongest purely neural baseline—suggest practical value in combining language models with symbolic search.
weaknesses: Evaluation consistency is a major unresolved concern. In Table 3, GPT-4o with oracle translation on Medium achieves 56.9% FPR but only 54.9% macro environmental pass rate. A final pass requiring all environmental and logical constraints cannot exceed the environmental pass rate under a shared denominator. The paper needs precise metric definitions, denominators, and corrected results.

The executable evaluator is insufficiently validated. Table 7's innercity_transport_cost references undefined variable 'node' instead of its argument 'mode'; innercity_transport_time defines a helper but never computes or returns a duration. The return-time example in Section 2.2 also contains inconsistent variables and uses equality instead of assignment. These may be manuscript errors, but runnable implementations and evaluator tests are essential when automated verification is the central contribution.

The authenticity and annotation quality of the human subset are inadequately documented. Recruitment, questionnaire design, filtering from over 250 respondents to 154 queries, annotator agreement, and resolution of ambiguous requirements are unspecified. There is no independent audit that DSL annotations preserve user intent, and feasibility verification for the human subset is unclear.

The comparisons do not isolate the source of the neuro-symbolic advantage. The proposed system receives handcrafted scheduling rules, search, and iterative syntax feedback, while neural baselines are mainly Act/ReAct. There is no comparable execution-feedback baseline, conventional planning baseline, or ablation separating heuristic search from LLM ranking. The five-minute search budget excludes LLM inference, and total latency, calls, and costs are unreported.

Claims about compositional generalization rely mainly on illustrative failures. The paper does not define controlled held-out compositions, quantify translation accuracy by constraint type, or separate linguistic difficulty from additional constraints and search difficulty.

Preference evaluation is limited to 50 easy queries selected because one oracle system already solved them. It reports no uncertainty or resulting feasibility rates. Improvements are mixed: preference-enhanced querying worsens both transportation-time measures, and preference-driven search does not improve restaurant transportation time over the baseline.

Reproducibility and real-world grounding remain incomplete: the manuscript provides no repository or dataset access link, concrete data sources and collection dates, or detailed routing simulation methodology. The DSL and solver largely combine established techniques, so the benchmark's contribution requires stronger validation and resource documentation to meet the acceptance threshold.

strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a meaningful benchmark gap: Chinese multi-day, intra-city travel planning with transportation, opening-hour, dining, accommodation, and personalized constraints. The environment spans 10 cities and thousands of POIs.

Combining 450 synthetic queries with 154 human-derived queries is valuable. Composable executable constraints and explicit preference objectives offer greater evaluation flexibility than a fixed inventory of requirement types.

The reported results suggest substantial benefits from integrating symbolic search: human-query final pass rates reach 27.9%, versus 2.6% for the best evaluated purely neural baseline. Oracle-translation experiments and failure examples provide useful preliminary diagnostics.
weaknesses: The central evaluation contains unresolved inconsistencies. In Table 3, GPT-4o with oracle translation on Medium achieves 56.9% final pass rate but only 54.9% macro environmental pass rate, although final success requires environmental success. The C-LPR equation also uses passed(C_p,p) inside a sum over individual constraints c, and its denominator includes all constraints rather than conditioning on environmentally valid plans. These issues require corrected definitions, reconciled results, and evaluator validation.

The published executable specifications undermine confidence in benchmark correctness. The return-time example in Section 2.2 uses inconsistent variable names and equality comparison instead of assignment. Table 7's innercity_transport_cost references an undefined node instead of its mode parameter, while innercity_transport_time only defines a helper and returns no value. These may be manuscript errors rather than experimental implementation errors, but the paper does not establish that the actual evaluator is correct or that its judgments agree with independent human assessments.

The realism and annotation quality of the human subset are insufficiently substantiated. The manuscript does not adequately document participant recruitment, questionnaire design, filtering from more than 250 respondents to 154 queries, annotation agreement, or adjudication of ambiguous requirements. The explicit satisfiability check appears in the synthetic-data stage; equivalent verification for the human subset is unclear. Consequently, low success cannot be cleanly attributed to agent limitations.

The comparisons do not isolate the source of the neuro-symbolic gains. NeSy receives domain-specific scheduling rules, search, executable validation, and up to five translation-refinement rounds, whereas the neural baselines are primarily Act/ReAct. Reflexion is excluded as a competing baseline despite being used within NeSy. There are no matched-budget validator-assisted neural baselines, strong alternative symbolic planners, or ablations separating handcrafted rules, LLM ranking, and search. A five-minute search limit excluding LLM inference does not establish comparable computational cost.

The compositional-generalization and preference claims exceed the evidence. There is no explicit held-out composition protocol, semantic translation accuracy, or quantitative breakdown of failure causes. Preference evaluation uses only 50 easy queries already solved by the oracle system, rather than representative human queries. Preference-driven search also continues optimizing while the baseline stops at a feasible solution, confounding preference representation with additional search. No uncertainty estimates or human preference validation are provided.

Reproducibility and positioning need strengthening. The manuscript supplies useful API tables and selected prompts but no identifiable code/data release link, detailed data provenance, complete agent prompts, or comprehensive inference settings. The DSL is essentially Python composition over domain accessors, and the planning pipeline adapts established translation-and-search approaches; therefore, the benchmark's contribution depends heavily on validation and accessibility that are not yet convincingly demonstrated.

strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a useful benchmark gap: Chinese multi-day, multi-POI planning with transportation, opening hours, accommodation, meals, and personalized requirements. The sandbox spans 10 cities and thousands of POIs.
The combination of 450 synthetic queries and 154 human-derived queries provides a valuable starting point for studying failures beyond templated requests.
Executable constraint composition and explicit preference objectives offer greater evaluation flexibility than a fixed inventory of requirement types.

Experiments across three LLMs, oracle-translation variants, and preference ablations provide useful initial evidence. The reported human-query final pass rate of 27.9%, versus 2.6% for the strongest pure-LLM baseline, motivates further investigation of neuro-symbolic planning.
weaknesses: Evaluation reliability has unresolved problems. Table 3 reports a 56.9% final pass rate for GPT-4o with oracle translation on Medium, exceeding its 54.9% environmental macro pass rate, although final success requires environmental success. This violates the stated metric relationship and needs correction or an explanation of differing denominators.

The published evaluator implementations contain substantive errors: Table 7's innercity_transport_cost references undefined variable node instead of argument mode, and innercity_transport_time defines a helper without returning an aggregate duration. The arrival-time example also contains inconsistent variable names and uses comparison instead of assignment. These may be presentation errors, but executable evaluation is the central contribution, and no independent validator audit or agreement with human judgments is reported.

Human-data validity is insufficiently established. The paper does not adequately describe participant recruitment, questionnaire design, filtering from over 250 participants to 154 queries, annotation agreement, or how ambiguity was resolved. Feasibility validation is described for synthetic queries, but comparable guarantees for the human subset are unclear.

The baseline comparison does not isolate the source of improvement. NeSy combines domain-specific rules, repeated search, validation, and translation repair, while the neural baselines lack comparable feedback and search resources. Reflexion is excluded for neural baselines but used during NeSy translation. Matched-budget comparisons and ablations of rule-based versus LLM-guided search are needed.

Claims about unseen composition rely primarily on illustrative failures rather than a controlled compositional split or quantitative semantic-translation analysis. The DSL and solver pipeline largely adapt established ideas; the benchmark's value therefore depends heavily on stronger validation of its distinctive data and evaluation design.

Preference evaluation is restricted to 50 easy queries already solved by an oracle-assisted system. It provides neither uncertainty estimates nor human preference validation, and Figure 6 shows regressions for some objectives. This supports a limited proof of concept rather than broad conclusions about preference handling.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript provides API descriptions and selected prompts but no repository or dataset access link, precise data provenance and collection dates, complete inference settings, or repeated-run statistics. Together with the evaluator and reporting concerns, these gaps prevent an acceptance recommendation.

strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a relevant evaluation gap: Chinese-language, multi-day travel planning with detailed spatial, temporal, financial, and personalized requirements. The ten-city sandbox and 1,154 human-authored queries represent substantial benchmark construction effort.

The executable DSL supports richer combinations of constraints than a fixed checklist. Separating environmental feasibility, logical satisfaction, and preference objectives provides a useful evaluation framework.

The experiments demonstrate a substantial advantage for the proposed NeSy baseline on Human-154: 37.0% final pass rate versus 2.60% for one-shot ReAct and 3.24% for the strongest reported LLM-modulo configuration. Oracle-translation experiments help distinguish translation failures from planning failures.

The appendices provide API specifications, constraint definitions, DSL implementations, prompts, search pseudocode, and participant recruitment and consent information. Human DSL annotations undergo several rounds of manual review.
weaknesses: The central evaluator lacks sufficient independent validation. Although Appendix J.5 describes manual review, the paper reports no annotation agreement, audited semantic error rate, or agreement between automated judgments and human assessments of itineraries. Some mappings lose important meaning: Figure 10 reduces food frequented by local residents to a regional cuisine label. Consequently, satisfying the DSL does not necessarily establish satisfaction of the original request. Explicit coverage of feasible witness itineraries satisfying both environmental and logical constraints is also unclear for the human sets.

The open-endedness and representativeness claims exceed the collection protocol. Participants receive descriptions of supported constraints and examples, choose from ten cities and restricted trip sizes, and queries that cannot be verified in the sandbox are excluded. Human-154 consists of student volunteers. This yields valuable human-authored queries within a prescribed ontology, but does not establish coverage of unrestricted real-world travel requirements; exclusion rates and unsupported requirement categories should be reported.

The main comparative evaluation is incomplete on the most important split. Human-1000 includes only NeSy and its oracle-translation variant, so the headline improvement over competing approaches is established on the smaller validation set rather than the test set. There are also no ablations separating the benefits of handcrafted scheduling rules, LLM candidate ranking, and symbolic search, or comparisons with strong non-LLM ranking heuristics.

The TTG comparison does not isolate limitations of the underlying approach from limitations of this adaptation. It restricts candidates to 22 POIs and uses one-hour time discretization, whereas NeSy uses a different search space and scheduling rules. These choices can alter feasibility. The explanation that solver pruning causes invalid solutions is insufficient: sound MILP pruning should not invalidate constraints represented correctly in the model. A matched-candidate comparison and an audit of formulation-to-evaluator mismatches are needed.

The compositional-generalization analysis relies on syntax-level pattern matching after POI anonymization. Semantically equivalent Python programs can differ structurally, so the reported low alignment on unseen DSLs does not directly demonstrate semantic failure. Behavioral equivalence tests on diverse itineraries and a controlled split separating linguistic variation from constraint composition would provide stronger evidence.

Reported results contain unresolved inconsistencies. In Table 3, oracle NeSy on Easy has FPR exceeding macro LPR for Llama and Mistral, which is impossible under the stated definitions because final success requires all logical constraints to pass. Appendix H.2 identifies DeepSeek-V2.5 and Qwen2.5-7B as the main experimental models, while the main text specifies V3 and Qwen3-8B. These discrepancies warrant an evaluation audit.

Preference evaluation is limited to 50 Easy queries selected because oracle NeSy already solved them, with no human preference validation or uncertainty estimates. Reproducibility is also limited by release being promised only upon publication and incomplete reporting of model versions, decoding settings, and runtime accounting. Together with the evaluator and comparison issues, these gaps leave the benchmark insufficiently validated for acceptance.

strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a relevant evaluation gap: Chinese-language, multi-day travel planning with detailed spatial, temporal, financial, and personalized constraints. The ten-city sandbox and 1,154 human-authored queries represent substantial resource-building effort.

Executable DSL annotations offer a practical way to evaluate compositional requirements beyond a fixed constraint taxonomy. Separating environmental feasibility, logical satisfaction, and soft preferences is useful.

The proposed neuro-symbolic planner shows substantial gains on Human-154: DeepSeek-V3 achieves 37.0% final pass rate versus 2.60% for one-shot ReAct. Oracle-translation experiments and translation-error analyses provide useful diagnostic evidence.
The appendices document APIs, environmental constraints, annotation review procedures, participant consent, search pseudocode, and several prompts.
weaknesses: The validity of the central evaluation requires stronger evidence. Appendix J.5 describes multiple annotation reviews but reports no independent agreement measurement, semantic error audit, or comparison with human judgments of itinerary satisfaction. Some formalizations lose important meaning: Figure 10 reduces food frequented by local residents to a cuisine category, while Section 3 treats avoiding spicy food as excluding entire regional cuisines. Such proxies can reject acceptable plans or accept unsuitable ones.

The main test-set comparison is incomplete. Table 3 evaluates only NeSy Planning and its oracle variant on Human-1000; ReAct, LLM-modulo, and TTG are absent. Consequently, the headline order-of-magnitude improvement is demonstrated on the smaller validation set, not the principal held-out human test set.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the source of NeSy Planning's advantage. It benefits from domain-specific scheduling rules, fixed activity durations, and structured search, whereas TTG uses 22 selected POIs and hourly discretization and LLM-modulo uses context-limited subsampling. There is no matched-candidate comparison or ablation replacing LLM rankings with simple heuristics. The five-minute search budget also excludes LLM inference, leaving end-to-end efficiency insufficiently established.

Claims of openness and real-world representativeness exceed the demonstrated scope. Participants receive supported constraint categories and examples, and queries unverifiable in the sandbox are excluded. The study does not quantify these exclusions or the resulting coverage bias. Moreover, unconditional rules such as prohibiting repeated restaurants encode benchmark conventions rather than universal feasibility requirements.

The compositional-generalization analysis relies on syntax-level pattern matching after POI anonymization. Semantically equivalent programs can have different syntax, so the reported low alignment on unseen structures does not establish semantic reasoning failure. Execution-based equivalence checks and controlled splits separating composition novelty from query difficulty are needed.

Preference evaluation is restricted to 50 easy queries already solved by the oracle-assisted system, followed by constructed preference variants. This selection does not establish performance on naturally occurring human preferences, and there is no user validation or optimality reference. The multi-preference extension remains a comparison within the same planning framework.

Reproducibility and reporting have material gaps. Release is deferred until publication. Table 10's supplied transport-cost function references undefined 'node' and requires a parameter omitted by examples; its transport-time function lacks an outer return. These may be documentation errors, but executable artifacts are needed to resolve them. Section 4.2 also calls DeepSeek best across all subsets although GPT-4o has higher non-oracle Easy FPR, and Appendix H.2 identifies different model versions from the main experiments. These issues, together with the evaluation gaps, place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: ChinaTravel addresses a meaningful evaluation gap: Chinese multi-day, multi-POI planning with human-authored requirements, detailed transportation information, and interacting temporal, spatial, and budget constraints.

The sandbox spans 10 cities and thousands of POIs, while 1,154 human queries provide substantially richer requirements than purely templated evaluation. The executable DSL supports useful compositional constraints and preference objectives.

The empirical results demonstrate a substantial advantage for the proposed neuro-symbolic baseline on Human-154: DeepSeek-V3 achieves 37.0% final pass rate, compared with 2.60% for one-shot ReAct and 3.24% for the strongest reported LLM-modulo configuration.

The appendices document APIs, constraint functions, participant recruitment and consent, multiple annotation-review stages, and baseline implementation details. Oracle-translation experiments and translation-error analyses help identify concrete failure modes.
weaknesses: The central claim of faithfully evaluating open-ended human needs lacks sufficient validation. Despite extensive internal annotation review, there is no quantified independent audit or agreement study establishing that DSL labels preserve user intent. For example, Figure 10 reduces restaurants frequented by locals to a regional-cuisine label, which does not capture the full requirement. Syntax matching in Figure 7 also cannot reliably distinguish incorrect translations from semantically equivalent programs.

The human data are elicited using predefined supported requirements and examples, and Appendix J.5 excludes queries that cannot be verified within the sandbox. This is a reasonable construction choice, but it limits the claimed openness and representativeness. The paper does not quantify these exclusions or adequately characterize the Human-1000 participant population.

Comparative evaluation is incomplete on the principal test set: Human-1000 reports only NeSy Planning and its oracle variant. The headline 37.0% result is on validation data; test performance is 23.3%, without competing-method results to establish the corresponding advantage. Missing ablations of LLM ranking versus simple search heuristics further limit attribution of the gains.

The TTG comparison confounds planning approach with a restrictive adaptation: only 22 POIs and hourly time discretization are used. The paper does not establish retained feasibility or separate approximation failures from solver timeouts. Its explanation that solver pruning causes constraint violations is insufficient. Likewise, excluding LLM inference from NeSy's time budget leaves practical runtime comparisons unresolved.

Several reported results require reconciliation. Under Appendix G's definitions, final pass rate cannot exceed macro logical pass rate, yet Table 3 reports 45.6% versus 45.3% for oracle Llama and 32.3% versus 32.0% for oracle Mistral on Easy. Section 4.3 claims PEQ improves five of six preferences, while Figure 8 shows four, and identifies the wrong transport objective as worsening. These inconsistencies weaken confidence in evaluation accuracy.

Preference evaluation uses 50 Easy queries selected because the oracle baseline already solved them, limiting generalization to authentic human requests and unsuccessful cases. Reproducibility also remains incomplete: release is deferred until publication, experimental model versions differ between the main text and Appendix H.2, and uncertainty across repeated runs is not reported. Together, the unresolved validation and evaluation issues keep this promising benchmark below the acceptance threshold.
